opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real tension there, and it took me a while to notice it in myself. Learning something feels fast. You read a paper, go through the code, and after a day or two you can explain it and feel like you understand it. Using it well is much slower. Using it means you've hit the edge cases, you've debugged it at two in the morning, and you know which parts actually matter and which parts are decoration.

With reinforcement learning, for example, you can learn the algorithm in an afternoon. The equations aren't that complicated. But getting it to work reliably on a new problem is a completely different skill. You need intuition for why the reward curve looks weird, whether a bug is in the environment or the training loop, and when to change a hyperparameter instead of the whole approach. That intuition only comes from repetition and from building things yourself.

So for me the learning part is the input, and the using part is where the understanding really happens. I'd even say you haven't really learned something until you've used it enough to be fluent in it. The gap between the two is mostly time spent getting your hands dirty.

That's also why I like building tools and infrastructure. When you write a library that other people depend on, you can't get away with a shallow understanding. Every abstraction you choose forces you to understand the thing more deeply than any tutorial would. Speed of learning is nice, but speed of use, meaning how quickly you can turn knowledge into something that works, is what really compounds over a career.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a tension I feel almost every day. Learning something fast is actually not that hard anymore. You can read a paper, skim a codebase, watch a talk, and in an afternoon you feel like you "get" it. The real gap is between that feeling and the moment you can actually deploy it under pressure, when the problem in front of you doesn't look like the textbook version.

I think of it a bit like the difference between reading about a training algorithm and actually making it converge on your own hardware. The first one takes an hour. The second one can take weeks, because that's where all the details you skipped over come back to bite you. Learning gives you the map, using it is walking the terrain.

So my honest view is that fast learning is mostly an illusion of understanding. Real understanding shows up in how quickly you can reach for the thing when it matters, without consciously thinking about it. And that only comes from repetition and from being wrong a few times.

What I try to do is shorten the loop between the two. When I learn something new, I force myself to build something small with it right away, even if it's ugly. If I can't use it within a day or two, it decays, and I'll have to relearn it later anyway. So I'd rather learn slightly less and use it immediately than learn a lot and use none of it.

astra-6.text: I think learning something quickly and being able to use it quickly are two different things. You can hear an idea and feel like, “Okay, I understand that.” But when you actually need it, you might still fall back on your old habits. So there’s a gap between understanding and practice. For me, the way to close that gap is to try using what I learn, even in a small way, before I feel completely ready. That’s also when I find out whether I really understood it.

sol-6.1.text: I think learning something quickly and being able to use it quickly are two different things. You can understand an idea when someone explains it, but applying it means recognizing when it’s useful and adapting it to a real situation. That usually takes practice. For me, the real test is whether I can use what I’ve learned without someone guiding me. So I try to apply things early, even if I’m not completely ready, because that’s often where I discover what I haven’t really understood yet.
